item.title: Modernizing the Developer Portfolio: Bento Grids, Proof Metrics, and Unified Theme
item.description: A comprehensive teardown and modernization of the portfolio and blog: replacing playful typography with authoritative developer styles, killing layout voids with a Developer Bento Grid, elevating proof metrics, and unifying the blog architecture.
item.author: jeffrey.jose07@gmail.com (Jeffrey Jose)
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Jose
item.content:encoded:
Seven months ago in episode 026, I overhauled this site's color system, migrating from an electric violet palette to emerald teal and introducing scroll-driven timeline animations. That redesign fixed immediate issues like broken keyframes and unstyled utility classes. But as time went on, stepping back to look at the portfolio revealed subtle signs of aging.

The personal website of a senior distributed systems engineer should communicate technical rigor, precision, and architectural discipline. Instead, several design decisions were working against that:

  1. Playful typography vs. systems engineering: The heading typeface (Syne) had wide, geometric letterforms that felt more like a boutique creative agency than someone who builds high-throughput Kafka pipelines and debugs WebFlux thread pool exhaustion.
  2. The empty void in Skills: The "Full Toolkit" rendered as a single vertical list on the left side of the screen, leaving more than 50% of the display completely blank on desktop viewports.
  3. Buried proof metrics: High-impact real-world numbers — handling 50k+ req/sec on WebFlux, scaling batch jobs by 3×, achieving All India Rank 170 (top 0.08% nationwide) in GATE Computer Science among 200,000+ engineers — were buried inside dense paragraphs where recruiters and hiring managers scanning in ten seconds would miss them.
  4. Header and mobile menu glitches: The navigation was a traditional block header, and the mobile menu had a transparency layering bug where menu items overlapped text directly over the hero.
  5. Drift between portfolio and blog: While the portfolio evolved, the blog templates remained anchored to the older layout, with disconnected navigation bars and an untextured dark background.

Here is how I audited, redesigned, and unified both halves of the website into a modern developer-themed design system.

1. Typography & Aesthetic Framework: Linear Meets Supabase

Modern developer tools — Linear, Vercel, Supabase, Cloudflare — have defined a recognizable visual standard: high-contrast dark backgrounds, micro-technical grid patterns, razor-sharp sans typography with tight tracking, and monospace accents for data and metrics.

Typography Hierarchy

I replaced Syne as the heading font with Inter and Plus Jakarta Sans, styled with tight negative letter tracking (tracking-tight font-bold). Headings now feel authoritative, structured, and legible at all scale factors.

For technical tags, episode numbers, status indicators, and metric callouts, I introduced JetBrains Mono. Code and metadata now look like they belong in a production IDE:

typescript
// tailwind.config.ts
fontFamily: {
  sans: ['Plus Jakarta Sans', 'Inter', '-apple-system', 'BlinkMacSystemFont', 'Segoe UI', 'Roboto', 'sans-serif'],
  heading: ['Inter', 'Plus Jakarta Sans', 'system-ui', 'sans-serif'],
  mono: ['JetBrains Mono', 'ui-monospace', 'Menlo', 'Monaco', 'monospace'],
}

Depth and the Ambient Micro-Grid

A flat black canvas (#09090b) without depth can feel empty or unpolished. To introduce subtle technical texture without clutter, I created a custom CSS background utility combining a 36px micro-grid with an ambient radial teal glow:

css
/* src/index.css */
.bg-grid-pattern {
  background-size: 36px 36px;
  background-image: 
    linear-gradient(to right, rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.035) 1px, transparent 1px),
    linear-gradient(to bottom, rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.035) 1px, transparent 1px);
}

Behind the hero and key headers, a radial gradient in emerald teal (rgba(28, 201, 160, 0.08)) provides atmospheric lighting that highlights the primary subject.

2. Floating Island Pill Navigation

The old top bar was a static full-width strip that felt heavy. I redesigned the navigation into a floating frosted-glass pill island:

  • Centered Island: Fixed at top-4, constrained to max-w-5xl, and floating above the content with backdrop-blur-md and bg-background/80.
  • System Status Indicator: Next to the brand logo (Jeffrey.Jose), an active monospace status pill with a pulsating green indicator displays backend.
  • Active Navigation Tracking: The navigation tracks the user's scroll position, lighting up the active section (Home, Writing, Experience, Skills, Projects, Blog, Contact).
  • One-Click Actions: A high-contrast Resume.pdf action button and theme toggle are integrated directly into the bar.

For mobile viewports, I isolated the mobile menu sheet using a dedicated popover surface (bg-popover text-popover-foreground border border-border shadow-2xl) with a fixed inset-0 bg-black/70 backdrop-blur-sm backdrop scrim, eliminating the transparency bleed once and for all.

3. Above-the-Fold Proof Metrics

Recruiters and engineers do not read personal websites sequentially from top to bottom; they scan for verifiable credentials within five seconds.

In the hero section immediately beneath the summary bio, I added a strip of high-density monospace proof chips:

  • 6+ yrs @ Jio Platforms
  • 50k+ req/s WebFlux
  • GATE AIR 170 (Top 0.08%)
  • IIT Kharagpur M.Tech

Additionally, the avatar now features a glowing emerald ring with a live pulse dot, signifying availability for high-impact distributed systems engineering opportunities.

4. The Developer Bento Grid for Skills

The most noticeable architectural change on the homepage is the Skills & Architecture section.

Previously, skills were split into a top card and a "Full Toolkit" list that collapsed into a single column on the left, leaving a gaping white (or black) hole across half of wide screens.

I completely rebuilt this into a balanced 6-card Developer Bento Grid:

Grid Area Focus Core Technologies
01. Core Architecture (Span 2) High-concurrency backend & event streaming Java 21, Spring Boot 3, Apache Kafka, Project Reactor / WebFlux, gRPC, Distributed Locks
02. Data & Storage (Span 1) Persistence, caching & search PostgreSQL, Redis, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Liquibase
03. Cloud & DevOps (Span 1) Containerization & orchestration Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, GCP, CI/CD, Prometheus, Grafana
04. Distributed Patterns (Span 2) Architectural resilience Microservices, Event-Driven, CQRS, SAGA, Circuit Breakers (Resilience4j)
05. Engineering Leadership (Span 2) Execution and quality Architecture Reviews, Mentorship, k6 & JMeter Load Testing, Chaos Testing
06. Verified Credentials (Span 1) Formal certifications Spring Professional, Oracle Certified Java SE 11 Developer

Every card in the grid uses a .dev-card structure with a subtle top-border gradient highlight (.dev-card-highlight) that activates on hover.

5. Experience Timeline & Project Window Chrome

Gradient Timeline Spine

In the Work Experience section (// 02. WORK EXPERIENCE), the timeline was upgraded with an illuminated gradient spine connecting all positions at Jio Platforms. Standout metric callouts (⚡ 3× Batch Speed-up, ⚡ 50k+ Concurrent Reqs, ⚡ 85% Manual Reduction, ⚡ 45% Incident Drop) were pulled out of prose into highlighted badges for instant readability.

macOS Window Chrome on Projects

For featured projects (like the scalable chat platform and TruthMeter AI), each card is framed inside simulated terminal / macOS browser window chrome:

text
● ● ● domain.dev DEPLOYED

This frames each project as an active, deployed engineering system rather than a generic card, highlighting architecture features, live demo links, and GitHub repository references.

Academic Distinction Banner

In the Education section, I created a dedicated achievement banner for GATE 2017 Computer Science AIR 170 (Top 0.08% among 200,000+ candidates nationwide), pairing it with my M.Tech research at IIT Kharagpur on distributed computing.

6. Unifying the Blog Architecture

A core principle from CLAUDE.md is: Portfolio and blog share one identity — if you change one, change the other.

Having modernized the portfolio, leaving the blog in its previous state would cause immediate visual drift. I audited the blog generation engine (blog/scripts/build.js) and its templates (blog/templates/):

1. Template Modernization

  • Fonts & CSS: Updated blog/templates/styles.html to load Inter, JetBrains Mono, and Plus Jakarta Sans. Integrated the 36px micro-grid and ambient top radial glow so reading an article feels continuous with browsing the portfolio.
  • Floating Island Header: Replaced the blog's block header in blog/templates/header.html with the same floating island pill design, complete with Jeffrey.Jose · blog brand status, responsive popover drawer, and ⌘K search shortcut.
  • Author Bio Card: Rebuilt the author bio at the footer of each article with an emerald avatar glow ring and live backend status indicator.

2. Fixing the Hidden { { inlineScripts } } Bug

During visual auditing with browser tooling, I checked the developer console on a generated post page and noticed:

text
Uncaught ReferenceError: inlineScripts is not defined

Tracing this down in blog/templates/post.html revealed line 571:

html
/* Inline scripts injected from frontmatter */
{ { inlineScripts } }

There was an inadvertent space between the opening curly braces: { { instead of {{. Because build.js uses new RegExp('{{\\s*' + token + '\\s*}}', 'g') for template interpolation, it required two consecutive opening braces. The template variable was never replaced, leaving { { inlineScripts } } as literal JavaScript syntax inside the <script> tag. The browser attempted to evaluate inlineScripts as an identifier and threw an error on every single post page.

Fixing this to {{inlineScripts}} resolved the error across all 38 generated post pages.

3. Trailing Slashes for Static Directory Routing

Static sites generated with folder-based permalinks (/blog/post-slug/index.html) require trailing slashes on URLs. When linking to /blog/post-slug without the trailing slash:

  • In production, GitHub Pages responds with an HTTP 301 redirect to /blog/post-slug/.
  • In local development or SPA preview servers (like Vite preview), requests without trailing slashes trigger history API fallback, landing on the React 404 page.

I updated all post links in blog/scripts/build.js, blog/templates/index.html, blog/templates/header.html, and src/components/RecentWriting.tsx to include trailing slashes (/blog/${slug}/), eliminating the redirect penalty and ensuring seamless navigation everywhere.

The Result

The entire site now presents a unified, cohesive developer aesthetic:

  • Clean builds: npx vite build, npm run lint, npm run build:prerender-harness, and node blog/scripts/build.js pass with 0 errors.
  • Hydration safety: All SSR / prerender constraints are strictly maintained.
  • Consistency: Navigating between the portfolio, the blog index, and individual technical write-ups now feels like exploring a single, meticulously engineered system.

item.title: TruthMeter 2.0: Deleting the Guesswork and Counting Only What Git Records
item.description: A year after shipping TruthMeter AI, I opened it again and found its core number meant nothing: any paste, any autocomplete and any file containing console.error counted as 'AI'. Version 2 deletes 19,000 lines and measures only verifiable evidence: co-author trailers, git blame survival, fix-within-72h and opt-in agent session logs. It is also the first release published to the Marketplace with no stored token.
item.author: jeffrey.jose07@gmail.com (Jeffrey Jose)
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Jose
item.content:encoded:
Working log for truthmeterai. Previous: Building TruthMeter AI: Measuring the Real Impact of AI Coding Assistants.

Episode 021 opened by complaining that AI vendors publish misleading metrics. "95% acceptance rate" means nothing if developers rewrite what they accept. I built TruthMeter to measure the real thing instead, wrote 4,500 words about it, and shipped it with 145 passing tests.

A year later I opened it again to update its dependencies. Before touching package.json I read the function every number in the extension depended on. It was producing exactly the kind of number that post complained about.

This is the story of version 2: what was wrong, what replaced it, and what the replacement says about this blog's own repository.

The function everything rested on

Every metric in v1 started from one question: was this edit made by an AI? VS Code has no API for that, so v1 guessed. This is the code from episode 021, unchanged:

typescript
private isAIGenerated(change: TextDocumentChangeEvent): boolean {
  const text = change.document.getText();
  const insertedLength = change.contentChanges[0]?.text.length || 0;

  // Heuristic 1: Large text insertions (>100 chars at once)
  if (insertedLength > 100) return true;

  // Heuristic 2: Pattern matching for AI signatures
  const aiPatterns = [
    /\/\/ TODO: Implement/gi,
    /function\s+\w+\([^)]*\)\s*{\s*\/\/ Implementation/gi,
    /catch\s*\([^)]+\)\s*{\s*console\.error/gi
  ];
  if (aiPatterns.some(pattern => pattern.test(text))) return true;

  // Heuristic 3: Rapid successive changes (AI streaming)
  const timeSinceLastChange = Date.now() - this.lastChangeTime;
  if (timeSinceLastChange < 100 && insertedLength > 20) return true;

Read each heuristic as a test with false positives:

  • Heuristic 1 counts any insertion over 100 characters. That includes pasting from Stack Overflow, pasting your own code from another file, and git checkout rewriting a buffer. A paste is not an AI.
  • Heuristic 2 is worse than it looks. text is document.getText(), the whole file, not the inserted text. Once a file contains one catch (e) { console.error, every edit you make to that file counts as AI-generated, including typing a single character.
  • Heuristic 3 treats two changes less than 100 ms apart as AI streaming. Accepting an IntelliSense suggestion, expanding a snippet and format-on-save all do that.

Everything else sat on top: churn, the "AI share" percentage, the ROI dashboard that turned hours into rupees. The research figures the post quoted were real. They were being multiplied by a number that meant nothing.

The 145 tests did not catch any of this, and they could not have. They checked that the heuristics returned what the heuristics were written to return. No test asked whether a paste is an AI. A test suite can only confirm a definition. It cannot tell you the definition is wrong.

The rule for version 2

One constraint decided everything else: count only what is recorded somewhere you can verify. If TruthMeter says a commit is AI-written, you can open the commit and see why. Where no evidence exists, the extension says it doesn't know instead of guessing.

That ruled out keystroke timing and pattern matching completely. What is left are four sources of evidence, each of which you can check yourself:

  1. Attribution in git history. Co-author trailers, agent bot authors and tool footers.
  2. Line survival. git blame at HEAD shows how much of that code still exists.
  3. Fix within 72 hours. How often a commit is followed by a fix or revert touching the same files.
  4. Agent session logs, opt-in. Claude Code and Codex record every file they edit, locally.

The rewrite deleted 18,957 lines and added 6,221. Webpack, husky, nyc, the ROI calculator, the keystroke tracker and three planning documents for features that never shipped are all gone. The extension now has zero runtime dependencies and bundles to 32 KB with esbuild. v1 was 2 MB.

Attribution: who says a commit was AI-written

AI coding tools increasingly sign their work. Claude Code adds Co-Authored-By: Claude … <noreply@anthropic.com> and a "Generated with Claude Code" footer. GitHub's coding agent commits as copilot-swe-agent[bot]. Jules commits as google-labs-jules[bot]. Cursor, Codex, Aider, Devin, Windsurf and Amazon Q all leave something similar.

Matching those looks trivial, but it isn't, because these tools have human names. A rule as loose as /claude/i on the co-author line flags a painter:

typescript
it('does not flag a human co-author named Claude', () => {
    assert.strictEqual(classifyCommit(human('docs\n\nCo-authored-by: Claude Monet <claude@monet.fr>')), undefined);
});

Jules Verne and Devin Smith had the same problem. The final rules anchor on something no human contributor would have: an @anthropic.com address or a model name for Claude, the google-labs-jules bot identity for Jules, devin-ai-integration or a Cognition address for Devin. Each signal also carries a confidence. A Copilot co-author trailer is marked medium, because it says Copilot was involved without saying how much of the commit it wrote. A bot author is high: the bot made the commit.

Rules are checked in a fixed order: custom rules from your settings, then agent authors, then trailers, then footers. A team that tags commits [ai-assisted] can add that as a rule without waiting for me. An invalid regex in a custom rule is skipped instead of crashing the analysis, and there is a test for that too.

Survival: is the code still there?

GitClear's churn research is the reason this matters. A commit is easy to count. What is still in the codebase weeks later tells you whether the commit was any good.

TruthMeter runs git blame --line-porcelain -w HEAD across the files those commits touched and counts how many current lines each commit still owns. Three details turned out to matter:

  • Only mature commits count. Code written yesterday has had no time to be rewritten, so including it inflates survival. By default a commit must be 14 days old, and the dashboard shows newer commits as "too recent" instead of as 100%.
  • The denominator is measurable lines. If a file was deleted, its lines count as gone. If blame was skipped for a file, because of the 400-file cap on huge repos, its lines are dropped from both sides instead of being counted as lost.
  • Lock files and build output are excluded. A package-lock.json change can add 5,000 lines. Without the exclusion one dependency bump would outweigh a month of real work.

-w matters too: without it, a reformat that only changes whitespace hands every line to whoever ran the formatter.

Fix within 72 hours, and the files everything touches

The second quality signal is how often a commit is followed, within three days, by a fix: or revert that touches the same files. It is cheap to compute and easy to explain.

On the first runs against real repositories the fix rate came out far too high. The cause was package.json. Nearly every commit touches it, nearly every fix touches it, so every commit "shared a file" with a later fix. README.md and CHANGELOG.md did the same thing. These hub files (manifests, READMEs, changelogs, .gitignore) are now ignored when looking for shared files, and the rate dropped to something believable.

Rates are also withheld when either group has fewer than five mature commits. A 0% or 100% from two commits is noise presented with a percentage sign.

Agent logs: the commits that don't say so

Trailers only work if they are kept. Plenty of people turn them off, and some repositories forbid them outright. Agents still leave a record locally, though:

  • Claude Code writes JSONL transcripts to ~/.claude/projects/. Every Edit, Write and MultiEdit tool call includes the absolute file_path and a timestamp.
  • Codex writes sessions to ~/.codex/sessions/. Its apply_patch calls contain *** Update File: headers, and the session metadata records the working directory.

With logs enabled, TruthMeter finds commits with no trailer whose files an agent edited in the 24 hours before the commit. They stay in the "other" group, since an agent editing a file doesn't prove it wrote the commit. The dashboard reports how many there are, as a warning that the AI share is probably understated.

This is off by default and turning it on asks for explicit consent. TruthMeter reads only file paths and timestamps inside the current workspace, never prompts or code, and nothing leaves the machine. Session logs are private data even when they are on your own disk.

What it says about this blog

The first repository I pointed it at, after its own, was this one. Over the last year:
Commits 173
AI-attributed by trailer 23
No trailer, but Claude Code edited their files within 24 h 18

The 18 are not a bug. This repository's CLAUDE.md forbids AI co-author trailers, and a git hook rejects them. TruthMeter has never seen that file. It found the gap from the session logs alone, and it reported those 18 as "other" with a caveat that the true AI share is higher. Counting both, at least 41 of 173 commits, about a quarter, had an agent involved.

Then a result I almost put in the wrong section. AI-attributed lines here survive at 67%, other lines at 38%. It reads like a headline: AI code lasts longer than mine.

It doesn't mean that. The "other" group contains the auto: rebuild blog commits that CI makes after every post. Those commits regenerate HTML in public/blog/, and the next rebuild rewrites much of it again. Generated output that gets regenerated on every deploy is about the least durable code possible, and it is all on the human side of the comparison. TruthMeter excludes dist/, build/ and out/ but not public/blog/, and it does not separate bot commits from human ones yet.

So the honest reading is that this comparison is confounded, and the tool did not warn me about it. That is the next feature: treat commits by CI bots as their own group. I would rather publish that than the 67%.

On TruthMeter's own repository the answer is simpler: 5 of 5 commits are AI-attributed. I wrote v2 with Claude Code, and the commits say so.

Testing against git instead of against itself

v1's tests mocked git and checked the heuristics against themselves. v2's main integration test builds a real repository in a temp directory and back-dates every commit with GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE:

  • six AI commits 35 to 40 days old, ten lines each
  • six human commits alongside them
  • a human fix: one hour after AI commit #3, changing one of its lines
  • a refactor 20 days ago that rewrites five lines in three of the AI files, plus a 500-line lock file
  • one AI commit two days old

That scenario has answers you can work out on paper before running anything. 60 AI lines are in mature commits, 15 are rewritten by the refactor and one by the fix, so survival must be exactly 44/60. One of six mature AI commits was fixed within 72 hours, so the fix rate must be exactly 1/6. Human lines must total 80, not 580, because the lock file is excluded. The test asserts those numbers. A heuristic can't pass a test like that by agreeing with itself.

The end-to-end suite launches real VS Code twice in CI, version 1.90 (the minimum supported) and the current stable, opens the same fixture repo and checks the commands, status bar and dashboard. That caught a problem no unit test would: mocha 12 is ESM-only, and VS Code 1.90's extension host loads tests with require(), so the whole suite died with ERR_REQUIRE_ESM before running one test. Mocha is pinned to 11, with a note in the repo saying why.

Building the webview turned up one more gotcha. The dashboard's comparison bars are sized with inline style="" attributes. If a nonce is present in style-src, browsers ignore 'unsafe-inline', so those attributes would be silently blocked. The fix is to use the nonce only for scripts and leave style-src with 'unsafe-inline' and no nonce.

Publishing in late 2026

The release workflow is the part of the project that changed most underneath me. Microsoft is retiring global Azure DevOps personal access tokens, and on 1 December 2026 they stop working for Marketplace publishing. The VSCE_PAT secret this repo had used since 2025 has two weeks left.

The replacement is trusted publishing: GitHub Actions requests a short-lived OIDC token for the workflow run, and the Marketplace exchanges it for a publish credential, but only after checking the token's claims against a policy you set on the publisher page: repository owner, repository and workflow filename. Nothing long-lived is stored anywhere.

I shipped 2.0.0 with both paths, OIDC first and the PAT as a fallback. The OIDC step failed with:

text
The token could not be exchanged for the specified publisher.

That was expected. No policy existed yet, so the PAT fallback published 2.0.0. After adding the policy (jeffreyjose07 / truthmeterai / publish.yml), I tagged 2.0.1 and the run went:

text
success  Publish to VS Code Marketplace (OIDC trusted publishing)
skipped  Publish to VS Code Marketplace (PAT fallback, works until 2026-12-01)
success  Publish to Open VSX

Then I deleted the fallback and the secret. Leaving it would have been worse than useless. The OIDC step had continue-on-error: true so the fallback could run, which means a broken policy would have fallen through to an expired token. The run would fail with a confusing 401 from the wrong step instead of the real error.

Two more details. The policy records GitHub's numeric IDs for the owner and repository next to their names, so someone who claims the name jeffreyjose07/truthmeterai after a rename can't publish as me. And Open VSX, which serves Cursor, Windsurf and VSCodium, still uses a token and a different publisher ID. The workflow rewrites the publisher field with jq, packages a second VSIX and publishes it.

By the numbers

v1 (Nov 2025) v2 (Nov 2026)
Source lines (excluding tests) ~5,000 1,452
Runtime dependencies 8 0
Bundle 2 MB 32 KB
Tests 145, checking heuristics against themselves 32, against real git and real VS Code
What "AI" means a guess from paste size, regex and timing a commit that records it
Marketplace publishing stored PAT OIDC, no stored secret
Time to analyse a repo — 1–2 s

Fewer tests and less code, but it measures something real now.

What I'd tell myself a year ago

The pitch was right. Vendor metrics are misleading, and churn and survival matter more than acceptance rates. My mistake was rebuilding the vendors' problem one level down: I needed a number, there was no honest way to get it, so I made one up and wrote thorough tests for it.

v2 often says less. A repo with no trailers and no agent logs shows zero AI-attributed commits and an offer to turn on session evidence, instead of a confident 37%. That is a less impressive dashboard. It is also the first version I'd trust with a decision.

The extension is on the VS Code Marketplace and Open VSX. The v1 settings (aiMetrics.*) were removed rather than migrated. They configured features that no longer exist, and the changelog says so.

item.title: Tuning a Fire TV and Two Phones Over ADB, and the One Setting That Broke Settings
item.description: One evening, three devices, all over Wi-Fi ADB. I disabled 15 preinstalled apps on a 2 GB Fire TV, measured a DNS ad-blocker and rejected it, checked my phone's battery wear and my wife's Pixel for malware. Every change was reversible. The only thing that broke was the setting I thought was safest: animator_duration_scale, which left the TV's Settings tile dead after a reboot.
item.author: jeffrey.jose07@gmail.com (Jeffrey Jose)
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Jose
item.content:encoded:
Our living room TV is a 43-inch Xiaomi FX Pro, Fire TV Edition. It runs Fire OS 8.1.8.5 (Android 11 underneath) on four Cortex-A55 cores with 2 GB of RAM. Menus lag, apps cold-start slowly, and the home screen is a wall of promoted tiles.

I spent an evening on it and on two phones, my Nothing Phone (2) and my wife's Pixel 7a, using nothing but adb from a Mac over Wi-Fi. Claude Code drove most of the commands while I made the decisions. It turned out that matters for one of the lessons.

The device changes were small. The process, and the one thing that went wrong, are worth writing down.

Rules before commands

Before the first command, I set three rules:

  1. Disable, never uninstall. pm disable-user --user 0 <package> stops an app from running or appearing without deleting it. pm enable brings it back in a second. On the Fire TV, which is not rootable on this firmware, a mistake with a system package could otherwise mean a factory reset.
  2. Write the undo before the change. Every disabled package went into a timestamped log, and a restore script that re-enabled everything existed before the first package was disabled.
  3. One change, then check. Disable one package, press Home over ADB, and confirm the launcher came back.

And a list of packages never to touch, whatever they look like: tv.launcher, firehomestarter, venezia (the Appstore), tv.livetv, anything in tv.settings.*, tv.ime (the on-screen keyboard), webview.chromium, the alexa* packages, and anything with ota in its name. Disabling the wrong one of those gives you a blank home screen and no keyboard to fix it with.

Connecting

On the Fire TV, ADB over the network is a toggle under Device & Software → Developer Options, and it listens on port 5555:

bash
adb connect <tv-ip>:5555
adb devices -l

Phones on Android 11+ use wireless debugging instead, which needs a one-time pairing. The phone shows a pairing port and a six-digit code. After pairing it advertises itself over mDNS on a random port that changes whenever wireless debugging restarts:

bash
adb pair <phone-ip>:<pairing-port> <code>
adb mdns services          # find the current connect port
adb connect <phone-ip>:<connect-port>

One trap cost a few minutes on the Pixel: the pairing dialog has to stay open on the phone's screen until adb pair finishes. If it closes, from a screen timeout or switching apps, pairing fails with an unhelpful protocol fault.

The Fire TV: 15 packages

I listed every enabled package, sorted out what was what, and disabled them one at a time with the Home check after each:

bash
r=$(adb -s $S shell pm disable-user --user 0 $p 2>&1 | tr -d '\r')
adb -s $S shell input keyevent KEYCODE_HOME; sleep 3
adb -s $S shell dumpsys activity activities | grep -m1 mResumedActivity

The first batch was twelve packages: Amazon miniTV, the shopping app, the game hub, the music and photos apps (bueller.*), the store-display demo content, two onboarding tutorials, a browser for casting web pages, ZEE5, sneakpeek (preview autoplay on the home row) and tv.acr.

tv.acr is the one I most wanted gone. ACR stands for automatic content recognition: on smart TVs it is the component that fingerprints what is on screen so viewing can be identified. The TV's ad settings were already all off. The package was still installed.

A second batch took out three more preinstalled streaming apps: Dailymotion, Fawesome and Mi TV+. SonyLIV looked just as preinstalled but stayed, because we actually use it. The TV's usage stats had no entries for any of the four, so "unused" was my claim to make, not something the device could tell me. A device can show you what's installed, but only you know what you use.

Animation scales, and the setting that broke Settings

Android has three animation speed settings: window_animation_scale, transition_animation_scale and animator_duration_scale. Setting them to 0.5 halves animation time, and the UI feels much quicker. On phones it's the standard first tweak. It changes nothing about how fast the device works, only how long it spends animating.

I set all three to 0.5 and read them back. The home screen felt noticeably quicker.

Then we restarted the TV, and the Settings tile did nothing. You could select it, press OK, and nothing opened.

I had just disabled twelve system-adjacent packages, so everyone, me and the agent included, suspected the packages. That theory looked good: some Fire OS components only show their dependencies at boot, and the Home check had only proven that the launcher could draw itself on an already-running system. A reboot rebuilds everything, and a missing content provider could plausibly block Settings. The plan became to re-enable all twelve and add them back one at a time with a reboot in between.

The system log disagreed before we got that far. The launcher was logging that it was finishing an activity "to prevent stuck menu". The launcher's slide-out menu waits for its open animation to finish before taking focus. With the animator running at half duration, that handshake no longer happened at the moment the launcher expected, so the menu gave up and closed every time.

Setting one value back fixed it:

bash
adb shell settings put global animator_duration_scale 1.0

On the next click, Settings opened, with MainSettingsActivity displayed in 211 ms. The twelve packages stayed disabled, and window and transition scales stayed at 0.5. Those two only affect how the system animates windows. animator_duration_scale changes the timing of every app's internal animations, including the launcher's, so it can break an app whose code depends on that timing.

Three things I took from this:

  • My check tested the wrong state. "Press Home and see the launcher" verifies a system that is already running. The bug only appeared when the launcher started fresh and read the new setting at startup. A change that a process reads at startup needs a restart to test.
  • I suspected the riskiest-looking change and ignored the one I thought was harmless. Animation scale is a tweak every Android guide recommends. Disabling system packages sounds dangerous. The actual cause was the harmless-looking one.
  • The logs beat the theory. The package theory was reasonable and would have cost an hour of reboots. logcat had the answer immediately.

Did it help?

Free memory went from 621 MB before the changes to about 710–740 MB after a restart.

That comparison isn't fair, and I'm not going to claim the difference. The 621 MB was measured after the TV had been on for a long time. The later readings came minutes after a fresh boot, and any Android device has more free memory just after booting. I didn't take a clean baseline after a reboot before changing anything, so I can't separate the effect of disabling apps from the effect of restarting.

What I can say: the home row no longer autoplays previews, ACR is gone, the app list is shorter, and with window and transition animations at 0.5 the UI feels faster. Whether it is faster I didn't measure, and that's the honest answer.

The ad blocker I didn't keep

The remaining annoyance was the promoted tiles on the home screen. Without root, the one practical lever is DNS: Android 9+ supports Private DNS (DNS-over-TLS on port 853), configurable per device without touching the router, so the TV could resolve through an ad-blocking resolver like AdGuard DNS.

Before committing to it, I measured lookups both ways from the TV:

Lookup Router DNS AdGuard DNS
Netflix, YouTube 6 ms ~44 ms
Hotstar, SonyLIV 6 ms 114–130 ms
Amazon Prime Video 6 ms 764 ms

Slower lookups are an annoyance on app launch. The second problem was worse. CDNs pick which video server to send you to based on where your DNS resolver is. Through the router, Hotstar's video edge was 9 ms away. Through AdGuard, which had no resolver in the country at the time, Hotstar sent the TV to an edge 43 ms away, almost five times farther, for every video segment of every stream.

That's a bad trade for the TV: the home-screen ads are static tiles that no longer autoplay or personalise. Free, ad-supported streams can also refuse to play when their ad server doesn't resolve. I rolled it back and left DNS on the router.

My phone: the number that actually matters

The Nothing Phone (2) didn't need speeding up. Its animations were already at 0.5, including the animator, which works fine on the phone. Nothing OS ships with very little bloat. So I checked battery health instead:

bash
adb shell dumpsys batterystats | grep -E 'Estimated battery capacity|Last learned battery capacity'

The battery's learned capacity was 3,592 mAh against a design capacity of 4,700 mAh, about 76% after roughly three years. Replacement is usually recommended somewhere around 70–80%. That one number explained the phone's shorter days better than any tweak could, and it means slowing further wear (charging to 80%, Android's adaptive charging) is worth more than anything else.

I also uninstalled 14 apps that I named myself from the list, with adb uninstall --user 0, and logged each one with its Play Store link. My rule here was strict: only apps I named. A long list of other candidates was left alone, including several multi-gigabyte ones, because large isn't the same as unused.

The phone also has a managed work profile, a second Android user. Nothing in it was touched or listed. pm list users shows it exists, and that was all I needed to know.

My wife's Pixel: the problem was storage

Her Pixel 7a felt slow, and the cause was obvious within a minute: 97 of 110 GB used. Videos took 27.5 GB, photos 22.7 GB, YouTube downloads 11 GB and app caches 6.9 GB. A phone that is nearly full has less room to work with, and no animation setting will change that.

The only change I made was animations to 0.5. Clearing caches would have been safe, since cache is data apps can rebuild, but she said not now. Which apps or videos to delete is her decision, not mine and not the agent's, so nothing was removed.

What I did do was check it for malware, because when a phone feels slow the next question is usually whether something is wrong with it:

  • Where apps came from. Every user app's installer was listed with pm list packages -3 -i, to spot anything not installed from the Play Store.
  • Play Protect was on.
  • Verified boot was green, the bootloader locked, no su binary, and the security patch level was from October 2026. Malware that could hide from the other checks would normally have to modify the system, and that would turn verified boot orange or red.
  • The permissions malware uses: accessibility services, notification listeners, device admins, draw-over-other-apps, usage access, always-on VPN, the default SMS app and user-installed CA certificates. Each was listed and checked.

It was clean. The phone is just nearly full.

Close the doors

ADB over Wi-Fi is a remote control for a device. Anything paired can install apps, read storage and send input over the network. When the work was done, every device got it switched off again:

bash
adb -s $TV    shell settings put global adb_enabled 0       # Fire TV
adb -s $PHONE shell settings put global adb_wifi_enabled 0  # phones

Then I confirmed that the TV's port 5555 was closed and that neither phone was still advertising wireless debugging over mDNS. Android revokes a paired computer after seven days without a connection anyway, but there's no reason to leave it open for seven days.

What I'd keep

  • Disable instead of uninstall, and write the restore script first. It cost nothing and meant every decision could be reversed in seconds.
  • Test a change in the state it takes effect in. If a setting is read at startup, restart the device to test it.
  • Measure before adding a "fix". The DNS blocker sounded like a clear win until it sent every Hotstar segment five times farther.
  • Find the actual problem. The TV needed less running in the background. My phone needed a battery. My wife's phone needed space. One fixed list of tweaks would have missed two of the three.
  • Use an agent for commands, not decisions. It ran every command, read every log and kept the restore script current. Which apps go, and on whose phone, stayed decisions for the people who own the devices.

item.title: The Keepalive That Was Disabled for Inactivity
item.description: In August I shipped a workflow to stop Aiven powering off my free Postgres. The event log says it lost: the write ping ran every six hours for twelve days and Aiven powered the service down anyway. Meanwhile GitHub disabled the whole workflow for repository inactivity on day 62 — an inactivity shutdown one layer up — and the API half never ran at all because its secret was never set.
item.author: jeffrey.jose07@gmail.com (Jeffrey Jose)
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Jose
item.content:encoded:
Working log for scalable-chat-platform. Previous: The Two-Month Outage: Dead DNS, Eager Filters, and Two Kinds of Postgres URL.

Episode 033 ended on a confident note. The app was up, the keep-alive was green, and I wrote that the health endpoint was "once again the first place I will look — assuming, this time, that something tells me to look."

Nothing told me to look. I went looking anyway, three months later. The fix I shipped in August had failed, and it failed in a more interesting way than "it didn't run": one half never ran at all, the other half ran perfectly and was beaten anyway, and the thing meant to supervise both was switched off by GitHub for inactivity.

Then I connected Aiven's management API and found out the outage I wrote about in episode 033 was the second one.

The scoreboard, and why it lies

In August I replaced a read-only SELECT now(); ping with a workflow testing two hypotheses about what Aiven counts as "activity." Then I pushed it and stopped thinking about it. Three months of run history:

bash
gh run list --workflow=keep-postgres-alive.yml --limit 400 \
  --json conclusion -q '.[].conclusion' | sort | uniq -c
text
 256 failure
  25 success

Every one of those 25 successes is in the first week of August, and the last is on 2026-08-07. My first reading was the obvious one: it went red when the database died and never recovered.

That reading is wrong, and the way it is wrong is the most useful thing in this post. The job was red for three months because of a missing secret in its first step, not because the database was unreachable. For long stretches inside those 256 failures, the part I actually cared about was working fine. A red job conclusion told me nothing, and I had trained myself to read it as if it told me everything.

Hypothesis A never ran, not once

The first hypothesis was that Aiven's notion of activity concerns the platform, not the database — the warning email says free services are powered off if "they or the Aiven platform aren't actively used," and the remedy it prescribes is logging into the Console. An authenticated API call was the closest programmatic stand-in, and I thought it the stronger bet.

yaml
AIVEN_API_TOKEN:
##[error]Set repository secret AIVEN_API_TOKEN (Aiven Console -> User profile -> Tokens).

Empty, on every run from August to October. The half of the experiment I considered most likely to be the answer never executed a single time, and I have no data about it whatsoever.

That is a design fault rather than an oversight. I wrote a step that fails loudly without a secret, handed over an instruction to create that secret, and built nothing that would notice if it never happened. In a run history, "never ran" and "ran and failed" render identically — both are a red X. I had 256 of them and could not distinguish the two states without opening a log.

An unset secret is an untested hypothesis wearing a failure's clothes. Worse: here it was also a successful hypothesis wearing a failure's clothes, because it masked this.

Hypothesis B ran correctly for twelve days and lost

The second hypothesis was that a genuine write might register where a read did not — INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, generating WAL and advancing the transaction id. I verified the SQL against a throwaway Postgres before shipping, and in my first pass at this post I wrote that it "could never have worked," reasoning that a powered-off service has no DNS record, so the write could never land.

That is true of recovery and irrelevant to prevention. Here is a run from 5 September:

sql
INSERT INTO keepalive_ping AS k (id, last_ping, ping_count)
        SET last_ping  = now(),
            ping_count = k.ping_count + 1;
 id |           last_ping           | ping_count

The write landed. It kept landing, every six hours. And the Aiven event log records what happened next:

yaml
2026-09-02T15:37:11Z  jeffreyjose.k@gmail.com  Powered on the service
2026-09-14T23:26:58Z  Aiven Automation         Powered down the free service due to inactivity

Twelve days of a WAL-generating write every six hours, and Aiven powered the service down for inactivity. The same thing had already happened in August: powered on the 15th, write ping running the whole time, powered down on the 24th.

So hypothesis B is not untested and not unworkable. It is falsified. Writing to a free Aiven Postgres on a six-hour cadence does not stop Aiven from deciding the service is inactive. Whatever that automation measures, it is not transactions.

This is a better outcome than the one in my draft. "Could never have worked" is an argument. "Ran for twelve days and the service was powered off anyway" is a result.

The event log is the only honest history

Episode 033's closing lesson was check the platform, not your config. I had been reconstructing this incident from GitHub Actions logs and dig. One call to Aiven's event log replaced all of it:

Powered on (actor) Powered down by Aiven Days up Keepalive in place
— 2026-03-07 — none
2026-05-19 (me) 2026-05-24 5 none
2026-05-27 (me) 2026-06-09 13 none
2026-08-01 (me) 2026-08-07 6 read-only SELECT
2026-08-15 (me) 2026-08-24 9 WAL write
2026-09-02 (me) 2026-09-14 12 WAL write
2026-11-10 (me) — — Aiven agent

Four things fall out of that table.

Every power-on in eight months was manual. Six of them, all with my address in the actor field. Every power-down was Aiven Automation, every one citing inactivity. Nothing I have ever built has recovered this database. I have been the recovery mechanism, running on an interval of "whenever I happen to notice," which the table measures at between five days and two and a half months.

There is no fixed threshold. Five, thirteen, six, nine, twelve days. In August I listed "the exact inactivity threshold" as the key missing number and assumed it was a constant I hadn't found. It isn't a constant. Aiven's own free-tier documentation declines to give a figure, and the event log shows why — the interval varies by a factor of nearly three.

The keepalive cannot be credited with the variation. The write-ping windows are the two longest of the four short ones (9 and 12 days), which looks encouraging until you notice that a window with no keepalive at all ran 13 days. With n=5 and a spread of 5–13, the variance swallows any effect. I can say the write ping did not prevent the power-off. I cannot say it did nothing, and I am not going to pretend otherwise.

Episode 033 documented the wrong outage. That post was about a two-month blackout, which the log dates to 2026-06-09 → 2026-08-01, fifty-three days. Directly above it sits 2026-03-07 → 2026-05-19: seventy-three days, twenty days longer, which I never knew about and which no post of mine mentions. I wrote three thousand words about my worst outage while a worse one sat one row up in a log I hadn't thought to read.

The finding: the monitor was disabled for inactivity

The run history stops on 2026-10-16. Not a failure — it simply stops, 25 days before I went looking.

bash
gh workflow list --all --json name,state -q '.[] | "\(.state)  \(.name)"'
text
active                Frontend CI
disabled_inactivity   Keep Postgres Alive
disabled_inactivity   Keep Redis Alive
disabled_inactivity   Ping app health
active                Dependabot Updates

disabled_inactivity. GitHub disables scheduled workflows in repositories with no activity for 60 days. My last commit was the keepalive experiment itself, on 2026-08-15 — and Aug 15 to Oct 16 is 62 days. The rule fired almost exactly on schedule.

So the chain reads: the free Postgres powers off because nothing used it for long enough, and the GitHub Action built specifically to prevent that is switched off because nobody committed to its repository for long enough. The watchdog was killed by the same kind of timer it was built to defeat, one layer up.

Neither policy is a bug. Nobody should burn cloud capacity on abandoned projects, and a cron job firing forever against a repo its owner forgot is exactly the waste GitHub's rule exists to stop. The failure is in the composition: I built a free-tier guard on top of a free tier and never asked what its idle policy was.

One more detail in that output. Frontend CI and Dependabot Updates are still active — event-triggered workflows are unaffected, only schedule: gets disabled. Every alarm I had was on a schedule. They all went quiet together, which is the worst possible correlation for a set of supposedly independent alarms.

What an Aiven managed agent changes

The fix now in place is an Aiven managed agent — postgres-health-monitor, running gemini-3.8-flash hourly, inside the Aiven project itself. Managed Agents is in limited availability; you request access per project and enable it once approved. Its instructions tell it to enumerate services, inspect health and node state, and restart any PostgreSQL service failing three consecutive health checks, with guardrails against destructive actions.

The important thing about it is not the model and not the remediation logic. It is the address.

Every previous version of this guard lived somewhere that could go idle: a GitHub Actions schedule in a repository I might not commit to, pinging a database that might not exist. The agent lives on Aiven's side of the boundary. It has no repository to go quiet, and crucially it does not need the database to be reachable to do its job — it talks to the management API, which answers whether or not any VMs exist. Both August hypotheses failed on placement rather than logic. This one is placed correctly, and placement is the thing that was actually wrong.

My prediction, written down to be falsified

The restart branch will rarely or never fire, and the agent will work anyway.

An agent that runs hourly and calls the management API to list projects and inspect services is, every hour, using the Aiven platform. That is hypothesis A — the one whose secret I never set — finally running in production, by accident, on someone else's infrastructure. The remediation is the headline feature; the heartbeat is the mechanism.

Note what the table above says about this: today's power-on at 14:29 was mine, not the agent's. The agent is minutes old and has recovered nothing yet. In eight months of event log there is not one automated recovery of any kind. So this prediction is live, and the event log is exactly where it will be settled — the next service_poweron row will name either Aiven Automation, the agent, or me.

Four things in those instructions worth a second look

I read the agent's system instructions against Aiven's documentation. Four mismatches, worst first.

The remediation verb may not match the failure mode. The instructions say to "initiate a service restart." Aiven's power cycle documentation describes three operations on this axis — power off, power on, delete — and restart is not among them. A powered-off service has had its VMs removed from the cloud; there is no process to restart. Recovery is avn service update SERVICE_NAME --power-on, which creates new VMs and restores from the latest backup, and can take "from a few minutes to a few hours." If the agent's tool surface offers a restart but not a power-on, the one scenario I built it for is the one scenario it cannot fix. And the event log confirms the state it will actually encounter is service_poweroff, not a sick node.

A powered-off service may not fail a health check — it has no health to check. The trigger is "three consecutive health check failures." A service with no nodes doesn't report failing nodes; aiven_service_get returns a state. Mine currently reads RUNNING with one node running. Powered off, there is nothing to fail three times. The condition worth watching is state != RUNNING, which is simpler and strictly more reliable than counting failures.

The 403 is about the agent's identity, not yours. The permissions error reads user_role_not_allowed_to_perform_operation, which sounds like it refers to you. It doesn't. Agents get their own Aiven identity — "the agent uses this identity, not yours" — with its own MCP role: read-only, read-write, or full access. Read-write explicitly cannot create or delete services; changing service configuration needs full access. A power-on is a service update. So an agent under-privileged enough to be refused the event log is very likely under-privileged enough to be refused the power-on, and it would discover that at the worst possible moment. That is a role to fix in the integration settings, not a prompt to reword. For contrast, my own membership on this project reads admin — which is why the same event-log call that 403'd for the agent returned twelve rows for me.

A system instruction is not a constraint. The 404 came from calling /v1/project/chat-platform when the project is chat-platform-db. The usual reading is that the model shortened a name from conversational context. What makes it interesting is that the instructions already forbid this, in as many words: "Dont ask the user which project to use — call the Aiven project-listing tool to resolve it yourself." The instruction to look it up rather than guess was present, and it guessed anyway. Prompt text expresses a preference. If a value must be correct, pin it literally or make the lookup the only path to it. aiven_project_list returns exactly one project here, so there was never anything to guess.

Three expiry timers, stacked

The agent is a better design than mine. It also sits on three clocks, and I would rather write them down now than rediscover them in a log:

Clock Length What happens
Agent MCP token 90 days Aiven-managed and not viewable; renewed by reconnecting MCP for the agent
Platform trial 30 days remaining $50 of credits, against non-free plans only
Powered-off service 180 days Service is deleted automatically

The second row has a wrinkle worth stating plainly, because I assumed otherwise before checking. aiven_service_get reports this service as plan: free-1-1gb, plan_price_usd: 0. The trial credits apply to non-free plans, so they are not protecting this database and the free-tier power-off policy applies in full. The trial is not a reprieve.

The 90-day row is this post's own lesson wearing better clothes. An agent whose credential silently expires in 90 days is a workflow that silently disables in 62. The failure mode is identical: the guard stops, nothing announces it, and the thing it guarded is fine right up until it isn't. I don't have a clean answer for that. The honest version is that every free or trial tier in this chain has an idle or expiry policy, each longer than my attention span and shorter than forever, and the only durable fix is the one I keep declining to buy.

Where it actually stands

The database is genuinely back — state: RUNNING, one node running, pg_version 15.19, and a fresh backup at 14:37 today. The backup list is its own little tell:

text
2026-09-13_03-54   42885294
2026-09-14_03-54   42936494
2026-11-10_14-37   42956974

Two days in September, then a 57-day hole, then today. Backups stop when the VMs stop; the gap is the outage, recorded in a field nobody thinks to read.

The correction: the app was asleep, not dead

I first published this section saying the app was down, on this evidence:

bash
curl -sS --max-time 120 -w "HTTP=%{http_code} time=%{time_total}s\n" \
  https://scalable-chat-platform.onrender.com/api/health/status

The first request returned zero bytes after 75 seconds; the second returned HTTP 502 in 9.3 seconds. Episode 033 built a taxonomy for exactly that — zero bytes means nothing upstream accepted the connection, a fast 502 is Render's own page for a container that died — so I wrote that the first request woke something and the second got the corpse, and I blamed the boot dependency.

That was wrong, and the Render logs say so plainly. Every boot in them completes:

text
Started ChatPlatformApplication in 157.503 seconds
Started ChatPlatformApplication in 80.699 seconds
Started ChatPlatformApplication in 82.792 seconds

No exception, no stack trace. The app boots fine. What I measured was a cold start on a free instance, and the dashboard explains why: the service runs on Render's Free plan, which spins down after roughly fifteen minutes without traffic — so render.yaml's plan: starter is still fiction, exactly as episode 033 found. Laid against my own requests:

Time Event
14:36:47 boot Started (157s); browser traffic at 14:37
14:51:47 last scheduler log, then silence
~14:52 spun down — last real traffic 14:37, plus fifteen minutes
15:04:56 my curl wakes it → boot Started 80.7s later
15:06:26 Instance restarted
15:15:23 Instance restarted
15:31 HTTP 200 in 5.1s

My probe was the thing that woke it. The zero bytes was an eighty-second boot in progress; the 502 was Render answering while that boot still ran. Nothing had died. As of this edit the app is fully healthy — HTTP 200 in 0.19s, all three dependencies UP, Redis at 66ms against the 4301ms I measured in August.

The symmetry with episode 033 is the part worth keeping. That post warned that a 45-second probe timeout against a 45-to-60-second cold start "produces failures that are indistinguishable from a real outage — which is precisely how a genuine outage hid in plain sight." Startup has since grown to 80–157 seconds. I wrote that warning down, published it, and then walked into it from the other direction: in 033 a real outage hid behind cold starts, and here a cold start impersonated an outage.

Two things in that table remain real problems. The restarts at 15:06 and 15:15 are genuine and I cannot attribute them — an OOM kill and a Render-initiated recycle look identical from inside the container, and -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 asks for a 384 MB heap inside a 512 MB instance, leaving very little for metaspace, code cache and thread stacks. Separately, Render's Health Check Path is still empty, three months after episode 033 called setting it "the single highest-value change on this list." Nothing probes the app, so a failed boot is never caught and a deploy is marked Live regardless.

The boot dependency I blamed is still a real design flaw — ddl-auto: update makes Hibernate connect during startup, so a container booting while the database is off cannot start. It just wasn't what I was looking at. Nor is it idle: the commit Render currently has live is eb20ccd, the August keepalive experiment itself. Nothing has deployed since, because auto-deploy fires on commit and there have been no commits.

That is the next piece of work, and most of it turns out to be configuration rather than code — the opposite of what I claimed when I first published this.

Lessons

A red check is not a signal, it is a prompt to read a log. 256 failures encoded at least three distinct states — secret missing, host unresolvable, and write succeeding while a sibling step failed — and the dashboard rendered all three identically. If a step can fail for a reason that isn't the thing you're monitoring, it will, and it will hide the thing you're monitoring.

Ask what the idle policy is of the thing you use to defeat an idle policy. Free tiers compose, and so do their timers. A scheduled GitHub Action guarding a free database is two inactivity clocks in series, and the shorter one wins.

A keepalive you cannot measure is a belief. I shipped a write ping, never checked whether it ran, and would have gone on believing it worked. The event log settled in one call what three months of run history could not.

On a free tier, a cold start and a corpse are the same observation. Zero bytes then a fast 502 is what a dead container looks like, and also what an eighty-second boot looks like from outside. Only the platform's own logs separate them — and a probe against a service that spins down changes the state it is measuring, so the first request is never evidence about what was there before it.

Move the watchdog outside the thing it watches, and prefer the control plane. The agent's advantage is not that it is cleverer. It lives somewhere that does not go idle and talks to an API that answers when every VM is gone.

A system instruction is a preference, not a constraint. The agent's own prompt told it to look the project name up instead of guessing. It guessed. Anything that must be correct should not depend on a model choosing to comply.

Read the vendor's verbs. "Restart" and "power on" sound interchangeable and are not: one acts on a running process, the other rebuilds VMs from backup and can take hours. Remediation has to name the operation the platform actually implements.

Check the platform, not your config — and then check the parts of the platform you didn't think to ask about. I ended episode 033 on the first half of that and still managed to miss a seventy-three-day outage sitting one row above the one I wrote about. render.yaml still says plan: starter. The event log, the workflow states, and the backup list tell the truth.

item.title: Four Reasonable Decisions and a Dead Feed
item.description: Every page on this blog advertised an RSS feed that returned 404. No single line of code was wrong — four independently sensible decisions composed into a file that existed only inside a CI runner. Plus a cross-domain sitemap, a verification file an SPA can fake, and what Hugo, Astro and Eleventy do differently.
item.author: jeffrey.jose07@gmail.com (Jeffrey Jose)
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Jose
item.content:encoded:
Working log for this blog. Previous: Documentation That Outlived Its Code.

Last episode I audited every Markdown file in this repo against the code and found that all seven described a site that no longer existed. The obvious follow-up was to point the same suspicion at the build system: not "does it run?" — it runs fine, 36 posts in about four seconds — but "does what it claims to produce actually reach the server?"

The first thing I checked was the RSS feed.

bash
curl -sL -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://jeffreyjose07.is-a.dev/blog/feed.xml
404

Every page on this blog has advertised that URL for months.

Nobody wrote a bug

The interesting part is that no line of code here is wrong. Four decisions, each defensible in isolation, composed into a file that only ever existed inside a GitHub Actions runner.

Decision one. The feed generator only runs under CI:

javascript
if (process.env.GITHUB_ACTIONS === 'true' || process.env.CI === 'true') {
    generateRSSfeed(posts);
} else {
    console.log('ℹ️ Skipping RSS feed generation (not running in CI).');
}

Reasonable-sounding: the feed embeds absolute production URLs, so why generate it on a laptop?

Decision two. .gitignore excludes it, filed under a stray # Vercel heading:

text
# Vercel
.vercel
public/blog/feed.xml

Also reasonable: it's a build artifact, and build artifacts don't belong in git.

Decision three. CI commits its generated output by directory:

yaml
git add public/blog/ public/assets/thumbnails/

And git add on a directory silently skips ignored files. No error. No warning. The feed is generated on the runner, staged by nobody, and evaporates when the job ends.

Decision four. The blog build is conditional, to avoid rebuilding 36 posts when only React code changed:

yaml
- name: Build blog
  if: steps.blog-changes.outputs.blog_changed == 'true'

Put those together and the feed exists in exactly one situation: a deploy whose commit touched blog/. Every other deploy publishes a dist/ with no feed in it. My most recent commit before this audit was fix(RecentWriting): show four posts — src/ only. So the live site lost its feed, and the three places advertising it kept advertising it:

html
<link rel="alternate" type="application/rss+xml" title="RSS Feed" href="/blog/feed.xml" />

Plus a visible footer link, plus a sitemap.xml entry submitting it to search engines with changefreq: daily — asking Google to crawl a 404 every day.

The control experiment was sitting right next to it. sitemap.xml is generated by the same script into the same directory and returns 200. The only difference: it isn't gitignored.

The generalisable rule: a file that is both conditionally generated and excluded from version control has no durable home. It exists only in the window between generation and deploy, and any path that skips generation ships a site without it.

The sitemap was lying too

Second thing I checked: rebuild with zero content changes and see what git status says.

text
 M public/blog/search.json
 M public/blog/sitemap.xml

Sixty lines of diff from a no-op build:

diff
     <loc>https://jeffreyjose07.is-a.dev/</loc>
-    <lastmod>2026-08-01</lastmod>
+    <lastmod>2026-08-05</lastmod>

The static pages were stamped with new Date() — the build date, not the content date. So every build told crawlers the homepage had changed when it hadn't.

Google's own guidance is that it uses lastmod only when the value is "consistently and verifiably accurate." Stamping today's date on everything is precisely how you teach a crawler that your lastmod is noise, at which point it stops reading it — and you've lost a real signal for the one time a page genuinely changes.

The same file also carried <priority> and <changefreq> on every URL. Google ignores both. They were so widely abused — everyone setting priority=1.0 on everything — that the fields became meaningless. Two-thirds of that file was decoration, and the remaining third was actively counterproductive.

Hugo solved this years ago with enableGitInfo: lastmod comes from the last git commit that touched the file. It's honest by construction, because the thing you're claiming (this content changed on this date) is exactly what git recorded. The one gotcha is that CI needs a deep clone, or every file reports the clone commit. This repo already checks out with fetch-depth: 0.

javascript
const out = execFileSync('git', ['log', '-1', '--format=%cs', '--', relPath], {
    cwd: REPO_ROOT, encoding: 'utf8', stdio: ['ignore', 'pipe', 'ignore'],
});

Local builds and CI builds disagreed

The search.json line in that diff was a different bug wearing the same clothes.

Three generators each sorted the shared posts array in place:

javascript
const sortedPosts = posts.sort((a, b) => b.episodeNumber - a.episodeNumber);   // index
const sortedPosts = posts.sort((a, b) => new Date(b.date) - new Date(a.date)); // feed
postsData.sort((a, b) => parseInt(b.episode) - parseInt(a.episode));           // json

Array.prototype.sort mutates. So each generator inherited whatever order the previous one left behind — and because the feed generator only ran in CI, the archive and sitemap came out in one order on my laptop and a different order on the runner.

That's the worst kind of build bug. It doesn't break anything visible; it just means git status shows phantom diffs you can't reproduce, until you stop trusting git status.

The fix is four characters: [...posts].sort(...).

What the mature generators do

Since I was already rewriting this, I read how projects with more users than me handle the same problems.

Astro's content collections validate frontmatter against a Zod schema at build time and fail loudly rather than deploying broken content. My build validated nothing. A missing description would have sailed through and rendered undefined into a meta tag.

I don't want a Zod dependency in a build script this small, but the idea is free:

javascript
for (const field of ['title', 'date', 'description']) {
    if (!frontmatter[field] || String(frontmatter[field]).trim() === '') {
        errors.push(`${where}: missing required frontmatter "${field}"`);
    }
}

The check that actually earns its keep is one no general-purpose generator could know about. Episode numbers here come from array position:

javascript
const posts = included.map(({ file, frontmatter, index }) => ({
    episodeNumber: index,   // ← derived from sort order, not the filename
    ...
}));

The 012- prefix in the filename is decorative. Delete one post and every later episode silently renumbers — in prose, in URLs, in the "previous episode" links that every post opens with. The invariant held across all 36 posts, but nothing enforced it. Now something does:

text
blog/posts/013-migrating-from-render-to-neon-postgresql.md: filename prefix 013
but sort position 012 — renumbering would change published episode numbers

Eleventy's preprocessor API drops draft: true content when RUN_MODE === "build" but keeps it visible while you're writing. I'd been carrying no draft support at all — every .md in blog/posts/ shipped the moment it existed. The convention transplants cleanly, with one wrinkle specific to this blog: drafts must not consume episode numbers, so the number comes from position in the full list while only published posts get rendered.

The RSS Best Practices Profile says content:encoded carries the article body. Mine carried this:

javascript
htmlContent = fs.readFileSync(postPath, 'utf8');  // the entire built page
const contentEncoded = `<![CDATA[${htmlContent}]]>`;

The whole document. <head>, inline <style>, the nav, the footer, the scripts — wrapped in CDATA, once per item. Even setting aside the size, it's the wrong content: a feed reader wants the post, not my site chrome.

It also emitted <author>Jeffrey Jose</author>, which is invalid — RSS requires an email address there. And lastBuildDate was a wall-clock timestamp, so the moment the feed became a committed file it would have churned on every single build. It's now derived from the newest post.

The part where I deleted five live pages

Adding drafts created a leak: a draft rendered by a local build stays in public/blog/ and gets committed. So I wrote a prune step — delete any directory that isn't a live post.

It worked. It also printed this:

text
🧹 Removed orphaned output: adding-text-based-visualizers-to-the-blog-homepage/
🧹 Removed orphaned output: building-a-scalable-chat-platform-with-claude-code/
🧹 Removed orphaned output: deploying-a-scalable-chat-platform-to-render/
🧹 Removed orphaned output: images/

images/ is an asset directory. The others are live URLs.

git checkout got them back, and the diagnosis was more interesting than the mistake. Four of those posts carry an explicit slug: in frontmatter that overrides the title-derived one:

yaml
title: "Adding Text-Based Visualizers to the Blog Homepage"
slug: ascii-visualizers

The directories named after their titles were left over from before those slugs were added — real pages, still served, duplicating canonical content. A fifth was published under an older title. My prune was right that they were orphans and wrong about the remedy: an orphaned URL that has already been served needs a redirect, not a delete.

So the prune now only removes directories git doesn't track, and refuses to run at all if it can't consult git:

javascript
if (tracked.has(name)) {
    console.warn(`⚠️  ${name}/ is published but no post or redirect owns it`);
    continue;
}

A build script that deletes things needs a definition of "safe to delete" that comes from outside its own inference. "Not in my current list" isn't it — my current list is exactly the thing that changed.

Those five stale pages are now redirects, which is a better outcome than either leaving them or deleting them.

Fixing the slugs, and paying for it

Which brings up the other thing the audit turned up: 11 of 36 URLs were sliced mid-word by a hard substring(0, 50).

text
/blog/building-a-secure-snake-game-with-terminal-aesthet
/blog/ai-as-learning-catalyst-how-to-gain-skills-without

Cutting on a word boundary instead is trivial. Doing it to published URLs is not — those paths have inbound links, and a static host has no 301.

The approach: blog/redirects.json is a committed, append-only record of retired URLs, generated by replaying every historical slug algorithm against every current title and recording what moved. The build emits a meta-refresh plus rel="canonical" stub at each old path, and CI fails if the file is stale:

yaml
- name: Check redirect map is current
  run: npm run blog:redirects:check

34 entries: 11 from the truncation fix, 23 from title and slug changes going back to episode 003 that had been quietly serving duplicate pages this whole time.

Determinism as a test

The check I'd have wanted from the start, now running in CI:

bash
BEFORE=$(find public/blog -type f | sort | xargs shasum | shasum)
SKIP_THUMBNAILS=true npm run build:blog >/dev/null 2>&1
AFTER=$(find public/blog -type f | sort | xargs shasum | shasum)
if [ "$BEFORE" != "$AFTER" ]; then
  echo "::error::Blog build is not deterministic — a second run changed the output."
  exit 1
fi

Two consecutive builds must be byte-identical, and a local build must match a CI build exactly. Both now hold:

text
local run 1: 6f2d1e27367c73695160baea06902053a0c26b1a
local run 2: 6f2d1e27367c73695160baea06902053a0c26b1a
CI    run 3: 6f2d1e27367c73695160baea06902053a0c26b1a

That single property would have caught the wall-clock lastmod, the mutated shared array, and the local/CI divergence — three of the bugs in this post — without my knowing any of them existed. It's the cheapest test in the whole build.

The sitemap nobody could read

Having made the sitemap honest, the obvious next step was to submit it to Search Console. That turned up one more instance of the same pattern — a file correctly generated, correctly served, and pointed at from the wrong place.

robots.txt said this:

yaml
Sitemap: https://jeffreyjose07.github.io/blog/sitemap.xml

Every URL inside that sitemap is on jeffreyjose07.is-a.dev. The apex github.io host 301s here, so the declared location and the contents disagreed about which site they described.

That isn't cosmetic. A sitemap may only list URLs on the host that serves it; when the two differ it's a cross-domain sitemap, and it's ignored unless both properties are verified and cross-submission is configured. So the one discovery mechanism that works without any manual submission was pointing crawlers at a file they would then decline to use.

Two changes: point robots.txt at the canonical host, and write the sitemap to /sitemap.xml as well as /blog/sitemap.xml. The root path is where crawlers and tooling probe by default. The /blog/ copy stays because it's already indexed — same generator, same bytes.

The manual route has also quietly changed. Google deprecated the sitemaps ping endpoint in 2023, and google.com/ping?sitemap= now returns 404. If you have a postbuild script still calling it, it isn't submitting anything. robots.txt and Search Console are the only two mechanisms left.

The SPA that verifies everything

Search Console verification for a URL-prefix property means hosting a file at a path Google names, containing a string Google names. It looks trivial. For a single-page app it is a trap.

This site's build ends with:

json
"build": "vite build && cp dist/index.html dist/404.html"

That's what makes client-side routing work on GitHub Pages: any unknown path returns the app shell so React Router can take over. Which means a request for a file that isn't there returns HTTP 200 with a complete HTML document. Not a 404. A confident, successful-looking page.

So the check that matters isn't "does the URL return 200" — it will, whether or not the file exists. It's whether the response is the file:

bash
curl -sL -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code}  %{size_download}b\n" \
  https://jeffreyjose07.is-a.dev/googlea374c01db1a7aeca.html
# HTTP 200  53b

curl -sL https://jeffreyjose07.is-a.dev/googlea374c01db1a7aeca.html \
  | grep -c "<!DOCTYPE html>"
# 0

53 raw bytes and zero doctypes. Had the file been misplaced, the first command would still have printed 200 — just with a few kilobytes of app shell — and verification would have failed with a "content doesn't match" error pointing at nothing obviously wrong.

Same lesson as the feed, one layer out: a 200 is not evidence that the thing you asked for is what came back.

Submitted, and the number is the point:

text
/sitemap.xml    Status: Success    Discovered pages: 40

40 is exactly what grep -c "<loc>" reported against the live file. When the artifact and the consumer agree on a count, the pipeline is intact end to end — which is a better result than "Success" on its own, because "Success" is just another green light.

Two episodes ago I was auditing docs that outlived their code. The build system had the same disease, one layer down: it said it produced a feed, a sitemap, a search index. Two of those three were lying, and the exit code was 0 the entire time.

Green builds are not evidence. Assert on the artifact.

item.title: The Two-Month Outage: Dead DNS, Eager Filters, and Two Kinds of Postgres URL
item.description: scalable-chat-platform was down for two months and I did not notice. A free-tier Postgres powered off, its DNS record vanished, and a servlet filter took the whole app down with it — including the health endpoint that was supposed to tell me. Now with the Render-side postmortem: a 59-day hole in the deploy history, an empty healthCheckPath, and one of my own conclusions falsified.
item.author: jeffrey.jose07@gmail.com (Jeffrey Jose)
item.dc:creator: Jeffrey Jose
item.content:encoded:
Working log for scalable-chat-platform. Previous: Hardening the Chat Platform: Deps, Deep Health, and CI Pings.

In episode 027 I added a scheduled GitHub Action that pings GET /api/health/status every five minutes and fails loudly if any dependency is down. That was the right instinct. Then it went red on 2026-06-03 and stayed red for two months, firing every five minutes into a void, and I did not notice until I went looking for something else.

This is the post-mortem. It has three stacked failure modes, each one hiding the next, and each producing a completely different error at a different layer of the stack. The interesting part is not the fix — the fix was one environment variable. The interesting part is why an app with a carefully built three-dependency health check could not tell me which dependency had died.

The symptom: zero bytes

The first thing I did was the obvious thing.

bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w "HTTP %{http_code} time=%{time_total}s\n" \
  --max-time 60 https://scalable-chat-platform.onrender.com
yaml
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 60003 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
HTTP 000  time=60.003420s

Zero bytes. That detail matters. A crashed-but-running Spring Boot app gives you a 500 with a JSON error body. A container that died gives you Render's own 502 page, and quickly. Zero bytes after a full 60-second timeout means nothing upstream ever accepted the request — the container was not listening on 8080 at all.

The CI probe had been saying the same thing for two months, in a more compact form:

yaml
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 45001 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
##[error]Process completed with exit code 28.

Dating the outage with gh

Before touching any config, I wanted two numbers: when did this start, and which dependency broke. The GitHub Actions history had both, for free.

bash
gh run list --workflow="ping-app-health.yml" --status success --limit 3 \
  --json createdAt -q '.[].createdAt'
yaml
2026-06-03T07:06:50Z
2026-06-02T06:51:40Z
2026-06-01T13:07:03Z

Last green: June 3rd. Then:

bash
gh run list --workflow="ping-app-health.yml" --limit 100 \
  --json conclusion -q '[.[].conclusion] | group_by(.) | map({(.[0]): length}) | add'
json
{"failure":99,"startup_failure":1}

Ninety-nine consecutive failures. But the genuinely useful signal was the other workflow:

yaml
